item.title: My Own Astro Theme Instead of Hugo and Blowfish - Why I Moved ProHomeLab to a Custom Engine
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: Why I swapped the off-the-shelf Blowfish theme for my own Astro theme, what it took, where AI assistants helped and where they got in the way, and how the site is published today.
item.content:encoded:
This is part five of my series on how the ProHomeLab site works. In part one I set up publishing from Obsidian through Forgejo, in part two I moved from my provider's shared hosting to GitHub Pages, in part three I tried squeezing everything into one repository with GitHub Actions, and in part four I gave up on that and went back to two Forgejo repositories.

All that time, only the delivery pipeline changed. The site itself stayed on Hugo with the Blowfish theme - I even have a step-by-step install guide for it. Now the site has changed too. Since November 15, 2026, prohomelab.com runs on an Astro theme I built myself.

Info

Article URLs haven't changed, I didn't touch the content in Obsidian, and publishing still starts with a plain push. Nothing changes on that side. I write in Obsidian, the Obsidian Git plugin pushes changes to the content repository on my Forgejo, that kicks off a build in a sibling repository on the same Forgejo, and the result lands on GitHub Pages, which hosts the site.

Below is why I did it, what absolutely couldn't break, how the work went, and what came out of it. In detail, including every snag I hit along the way.

Why I didn't stay on Blowfish

The honest answer sounds a bit childish. I just can't sit still. If something works, I still want to make it better, even though I'm old enough to know that if it ain't broke, you don't fix it. But behind that itch there are some very concrete reasons.

Someone else's theme is always someone else's

Blowfish is a good theme. No - a very good theme. It's fast, it ships a huge set of shortcodes and visual effects, and the docs are decent. But it's someone else's product with someone else's decisions baked in. As long as your site looks like the theme's demo, life is great. The moment you want to do things your own way, you start fighting it.

Before the move I audited my Hugo repository. My own code came to about 1,200 lines, and a good chunk of it was copies of theme files with my changes on top:

File What was in it
layouts/_default/single.html a copy of the Blowfish 3.8.0 article template plus a dark strip with a YouTube player above the text
layouts/partials/schema.html a copy of the search-engine markup plus a VideoObject type for videos
assets/js/code.js a copy of the theme script, just to get a different copy-code button
assets/css/custom.css 331 lines of my own styles layered over the theme

Every one of those copies is a time bomb. The theme moved to 3.9.0, while my single.html still carried 3.8.0 logic. Working out what changed upstream and what's now broken on my side is a fresh investigation every single time. On top of that, Hugo templates aren't exactly fun to edit - Go template logic full of dots, with and range is hard to read. And if, like me, you're not a web designer, not a front-end developer, basically a muggle, making it all look good drifts into science fiction.

Every Hugo site looks vaguely the same

The second thing that bugged me was how recognizable it all is. Open ten blogs on Blowfish, PaperMod or Congo, and you'll know what they're built with almost instantly. Header, cards, spacing, typography - all out of the same box. Ready-made themes also draw lines you can't cross without copying their templates.

And now there's a second wave of sameness on top of that - AI-made design. Purple-to-blue gradients, glassy cards, glows, emoji in headings, identical rounded tiles. Once your eye is trained, you can even tell which model made it from the colors and fonts. I'm sick of it, and I definitely didn't want my site looking like that. I'll come back to this later.

My history with Astro themes

This isn't my first time with Astro. Between the first and second Blowfish versions of the site there was a stretch on Astro with the Twilight theme, and before that I'd looked at Fuwari. That era is exactly why some articles still have old URLs that I later had to add to aliases.

The real problem with those themes isn't Astro, it's how they're built. They're starter templates. You clone the theme's repository, and it becomes your site. Theme code, your settings and your content all live in one pile. A theme update comes out - and you have to merge it into your fork by hand, while the update happily, and with a little smack of the lips, overwrites your settings. Both themes are also built primarily for a Chinese audience, and you feel it everywhere, from the fonts to the set of integrations.

So the core requirement for my own theme was clear from day one. The theme has to be a package, like any other dependency, and the site is just a user of that package. The site configures the theme and swaps out individual components when it needs to, but never touches the theme's code. Updating the theme is a plain npm update, not a branch merge.

I want more than a blog

On Hugo, anything more complex than an article is, let's say, a pain in a certain place. And I have plans for interactive things right on the site - I want to build in a calculator for 10-inch racks, for example - plus a separate news section for homelab and self-hosting. Astro has islands for exactly this - interactive components that load their JavaScript only where they're needed, while the rest of the page stays plain HTML.

Not just for me

And finally, I want the theme to be a product of its own that can go up on GitHub and npm for others to build on. Plenty of people write in Obsidian, run a blog in more than one language and fight the same battles I do. So from the start the theme wasn't made "for ProHomeLab" but for any author. The ProHomeLab site is just its first user - if a site can be called a user, of course. If a feature isn't used in my articles but others would need it, it still gets built completely and tested on the demo site.

What Astro is

Astro is an open-source web framework for content-first sites - blogs, documentation, project sites. Like Hugo, it builds the site ahead of time, and what you get are ordinary HTML files you can put on any host. The difference is in how the site itself is made. Hugo is a single Go binary with Go templates, while Astro runs on Node.js, installs through npm, and builds pages out of components. An .astro component looks like an HTML file with JavaScript mixed in, and that JavaScript runs only at build time - it never reaches the browser. Code goes to the browser only when you explicitly ask for it, for example on an interactive block with a client:load or client:visible directive. Those blocks are called islands. You can write an island in Astro itself or in React, Vue or Svelte, and the rest of the page stays static HTML with no extra scripts. You don't need a server either. Astro can render pages on a server on demand, but my site is built fully static and served from GitHub Pages, same as before. If you're curious who else runs on it, take a look at the Astro showcase - there are plenty of big names there.

Why Astro

I could have written my own theme for Hugo too. But I figured that if I'm walking away from someone else's code, I might as well walk away from awkward templates as well. Here's what Astro gives me:

  • Components instead of templates. A page's markup, data and styles live in one readable .astro file instead of being smeared across partials.
  • Content collections with a schema. Article front matter is validated at build time. A typo in a date or a link to a missing cover stops the build with a clear error, instead of turning into an image that quietly vanished from the site. And I might never find out about a missing image, because readers don't write in about things like that.
  • An integrations API. The theme can be packaged as an integration - a package that adds pages, Markdown processing, types and scripts to the site by itself. That's exactly what a "theme as a package" setup needs.
  • Static builds. The output is plain files served from GitHub Pages, the same way Hugo's output used to be. No server.

The work was done on Astro 7.4. Markdown goes through Unified (remark and rehype), because that's where the plugins I need live - for directives and Obsidian wiki links, for example.

What couldn't break

Before writing any code, I made a list of things without which the move made no sense.

URLs. This is the big one. YouTube, Telegram, other sites and search engines all link to my articles. Every engine change I've done before ended with a pile of 404s in Google Search Console. This time not a single public URL was allowed to disappear.

Content from Obsidian, untouched. Articles live in Obsidian and sync to Forgejo, as I described in my post about my process from note to article. Blowfish-style front matter, {{< mermaid >}} and {{< alert >}} shortcodes, ![[...]] embeds, relative image paths - all of it had to work as is, without mass edits, ideally without any edits at all.

Two languages, done properly. A translation is a separate index.en.md file, versions are linked for search engines (hreflang), and the language switcher only points where a translation actually exists.

Everything Blowfish did. Breadcrumbs, a table of contents that highlights the current section, reading progress, series, related posts, tags and categories, search, RSS, sitemap, reading mode, dark mode.

Publishing the same way. Push to the content repository, build in Forgejo Actions, deploy to GitHub Pages.

How the work went

First, the elephant in the room - the thing many will ask about and even more will think.

I'm not a designer or a front-end developer

I can't write front-end code at the level I wanted for the site, and I can't design interfaces. So the theme's code was written by AI assistants - Claude Code and, oddly enough, Codex. I made the decisions, and I checked the results.

Let me be clear up front, so there are no illusions. This was not "hey, make me a website." I already had a finished site with its own design, which I'd spent ages polishing, its own blocks and its own markup, and the job was to move all of it to a new framework without losing anything. I knew exactly how everything worked on Hugo, I knew exactly what I wanted, and, more importantly, what I didn't want under any circumstances. Every step came with a long list of requirements, then review and fixes, then more fixes. Just porting what was essentially a finished theme took more than 24 hours of continuous work with the AI (yes, I timed it), and that's not counting my own reviews and decisions between steps.

To put it bluntly, left unsupervised, AI produces exactly the kind of design that makes me recoil. Ask for "a modern blog site" and you'll get gradients, glows and frosted-glass panels. Claude, for one, loves its native terracotta. On Blowfish my buttons were honey amber, which I think looks great - but who's going to notice the difference? So I kept slapping their hands as hard as I could.

  • Fonts and colors only after discussion. No freelancing. The colors come from the ProHomeLab brand book in its "quiet" variant (that's my own internal term) - graphite, neutral links, mint only in small details, gradients only as a thin line, amber only as a dot in the logo. Headings and body text are set in Geologica, code in JetBrains Mono. Unbounded, which used to be on the site and in the logo, is gone completely. It's everywhere right now and looks AI-made on its own, even when no AI was involved.
  • No decoration for decoration's sake. No particles, no mascots, no animation on every block, no hero section with a shimmering background.
  • Checked against rules, not by eye. Line length, button size, contrast and heading order were checked against accessibility guidelines. For example, the guideline says a line should be 65-75 characters, while I wanted wider text for density. The AI and I settled on a compromise - 79 characters on average. It's a deliberate deviation, not an accident. Or, well, there are no accidents.
  • Compared against the old site. Text width, page density and phone behavior were compared with Blowfish by the numbers at different screen widths. That took me a lot of time, especially since my phone has a narrow, tall screen.

The assistants made mistakes along the way, and not obvious ones. Here are two that only surfaced because of the checks. On Windows the file system ignores letter case, so a redirect from the old URL /posts/Name/ silently overwrote the article at /posts/name/ itself. Nine Russian articles vanished that way, and I didn't notice right away - the URL still answered, it just served a redirect instead of the article. After that, the URL check script learned to tell a real article from a redirect page. The other one was the language suggestion. If a reader picked English and then clicked "RU" in the "Other languages" block under the title, they got bounced straight back to English. That one was caught while checking in the browser, before it went live.

That's my main takeaway about working with AI. It speeds up everything except checking. You have to check more, not less. And ironically, you end up spending more time than if you'd done it all yourself (assuming, of course, that you could do it all yourself).

Order of work

The work went in phases, with the riskiest parts checked first:

  1. Skeleton - the theme package, a single article page, a demo site, the first documentation page.
  2. Parity with the current site - everything ProHomeLab needs, plus the URL check. No switch-over without it.
  3. Switch-over - only once the URL check reports zero mismatches, and after I've looked it over myself.
  4. New stuff - news, interactive tools, link-preview images.
  5. Public release - GitHub, npm, versioning.

Every decision that had alternatives got its own note with the context, the options and the conclusion. There are thirteen of them so far. Every step is a separate entry in a journal in Obsidian. I'll keep quiet about how much text that adds up to - I think you get a sense of the amount of work. That's my answer to the clickbait videos where an AI builds someone a website in five minutes (and forgets to explain how any of it works). The theme's documentation was written alongside the code, in parallel really, and a feature without a docs page and a demo example didn't count as done. I set myself that rule on day one, because the theme is meant to go public, and nobody wants to dig through undocumented code later, me included.

On the calendar, the first two phases plus the switch-over fit into two days. But behind those two days are more than a full day of non-stop AI work and dozens of "requirements, result, review, fixes" loops on my side. I'd make a joke about being a meat proxy, but I'm the one who set the task, too. The only fast part here is that the assistant doesn't get tired - the usage limits do. Deciding, checking and sending things back for rework was all on me, and boy, is it exhausting.

The URL check

This is the most useful part of the whole move, and it deserves its own section.

I didn't trust the sitemap. It leaves out tag pages, redirects from old URLs and RSS feeds. Instead, I built the whole Hugo site into a temporary folder on Windows and turned the output into a complete list of URLs with their types. That came to 1,338 URLs. Even I was surprised.

Here's how it broke down. 702 of them are Hugo by-products that nothing links to:

  • an automatic /page/1/ redirect for every list and every tag - 348 of them
  • a separate RSS feed for every section and tag - 352
  • the Blowfish search index index.json - 2

I decided not to reproduce those. That left 636 public URLs that actually get used - articles, sections, tag, category and series pages, the main feeds, the sitemap, robots.txt, and 76 old URLs from aliases that have to point to the new ones.

The check script makes sure the new build serves every one of the 636 URLs, and that an article is an actual article, not a redirect. If anything is missing, the script exits with an error. The same script now runs in the Forgejo build, so the site won't publish if a URL goes missing, and I immediately know where I messed up. Or where someone else did. The number of mismatches was the main progress metric for that phase, and the switch-over only started when it hit zero.

The safety net is the 404 report in Search Console. If one of the dropped URLs turns out to matter to someone, it'll show up there, I'll see it and add it to aliases.

What I ended up with

The theme does everything Blowfish did on my site, and a bit more. Here's what readers can see.

Articles. A cover or a YouTube video above the text, a table of contents that highlights the current section, reading progress, series, related posts, previous and next, share buttons, reading mode, an author box. On wide screens, tables and screenshots spill out of the text column into the free space, while the text itself stays at a comfortable width.

Lists and taxonomies. "All articles" grouped by year, sections from folders, pinned posts, tags, categories, series, author pages. Tag URLs follow the same rules as Hugo, so they matched without any manual work.

Markup. Blowfish shortcodes work as is (and remember, this is a different framework), and each one also has a second syntax for new content. Obsidian- and GitHub-style callouts, math, Mermaid diagrams, Obsidian embeds, repository cards, galleries, tabs, steps.

Search. Pagefind, a separate index per language, no server. Open it with the button in the header or the / key.

Languages. If your browser isn't set to Russian (I count Ukrainian, Belarusian and Kazakh as Russian too, since readers there usually read Russian), a strip appears at the top saying "This page is available in English", with buttons. Nobody gets redirected automatically - that's Google's recommendation. Your choice is remembered. The analytics banner speaks your language too.

A 404 page in both languages, suggesting similar articles based on the words in the broken URL.

View counts. View counts and likes used to run on Firebase. I dropped Firebase and the likes. That was a whim - back when I was starting out, I somehow thought it was a useful bit of eye candy. I've grown up and realized I don't need it. View counts now come from my self-hosted Umami on every build and are written straight into the pages, so your browser doesn't go anywhere to fetch them. The downside is that my Umami has only been running since October 2026, so the numbers are lower than before.

Note

Just in case, for the especially curious. My Umami's own address never shows up on the site. Your browser loads the tracker from stats.prohomelab.com, which is a Cloudflare Worker - more on that below. The internal address the build uses to fetch view counts only lives in the build settings, too.

Consent-based analytics. Yandex Metrica, Google Analytics and Umami don't load until you click "Accept". Both buttons, "Accept" and "Decline", look exactly the same, so nobody gets nudged into agreeing. I don't do that kind of thing.

Phone first. Styles are written for narrow screens and expand for wide ones. At 360 px no page scrolls sideways, and buttons are at least 44 px. Every feature was checked on a phone and on a desktop before it counted as done. Then again, who am I kidding? I'm still catching small bugs.

How articles get published now

The flow is the same as in part four, only the players changed.

  1. I write an article in Obsidian, and Obsidian Git pushes it to the content repository on Forgejo
  2. A small workflow in the content repository calls the build in the site repository through the API
  3. The build on the Forgejo runner pulls the site, the theme and the articles, installs dependencies with npm ci, builds the site, fetches view counts from Umami and checks all 636 URLs
  4. If everything's fine, the folder with the finished site goes to the gh-pages branch of a new GitHub repository, and GitHub Pages serves it on prohomelab.com

A clean build takes a little over two minutes.

Along the way there were a few moments that were interesting and educational, at least for me.

Umami behind Authentik. The public address of my Umami sits behind Authentik, with only the tracking script and the stats endpoint left open - without them the counter simply wouldn't work for readers. The build, trying to log in to the Umami API, got the Authentik login page instead of an answer. I don't want to expose the API to the outside world. So the build talks to Umami over its internal address, bypassing the proxy, and that address lives in a Forgejo variable. Umami got a separate user with view-only rights for this.

The firewall. The next attempt failed with fetch failed. The runner and Umami live on different subnets with rules between them. Ping went through, but connections to the port were dropped. One rule fixed it - the runner is allowed to reach a single Umami port, and nothing else.

A separate address for the tracker. Your browser loads the tracking script directly, so its address is visible in the source of any page. It used to be my Umami's own domain, and I didn't want that out in the open. Now a tiny Cloudflare Worker on stats.prohomelab.com sits between the site and Umami. It lets exactly five paths through - the two scripts, the page-view endpoint, the session-recording endpoint and its settings - and answers 404 to everything else, the dashboard login included. The Worker hands the reader's address to Umami in a separate header, but only for two things - looking up the country and city in Umami's own GeoLite database, and telling one visit from another. Umami doesn't store the IP itself (its database doesn't even have a field for it) and never shows it to me; all I see in the stats is the country, city, browser and device. Without that header, every visitor would appear to be wherever the Worker happens to run. Cloudflare's free tier covers this with room to spare. I tested it with a visit from my phone - it showed up in Umami right away, with the correct country, the one the phone was actually connecting from.

First runs without publishing. The deploy-to-GitHub step only kicks in once a target repository is configured. The first runs on the real runner built and checked the site without touching the live one. I highly recommend doing this for any migration.

Switching the domain

The move itself took a few minutes. What mattered was the order.

First I redirected the build. The old Hugo build pushed a CNAME file with my domain to the old repository on every new article. If it had fired after the move, GitHub could have handed the domain back to the old repository. So first the workflow in the content repository started calling the new build, and only then did I move the domain.

Moving it in GitHub Pages means removing the domain in the old repository's settings and entering it in the new one. No DNS changes needed, since both repositories belong to the same account. The certificate was issued right away. Articles started loading from the new site almost instantly, while the home page kept coming from GitHub's CDN cache for a few more minutes.

After the move, the script walked through all 636 URLs on the live domain. Every one answered.

I'm not deleting the old build or the old repository yet. Rolling back means moving the domain back and reverting one line in the workflow - a couple of minutes' work. In a few weeks, once it's clear I won't need it, the old site will be shut down for good.

What isn't perfect

It wouldn't be honest to end on the good parts only.

  • The theme isn't published yet. It lives in my private Forgejo. A public release on GitHub and npm is a separate phase, and until then the theme isn't ready for other people's sites.
  • The documentation is English-only. There's no Russian version apart from the home page. No offense to anyone, but I don't see the point of Russian docs yet, even though, for obvious reasons, they'd be easier for me to write.
  • Publishing under a subfolder isn't supported. The site has to live at the root of a domain. An address like user.github.io/repo/ doesn't work yet.
  • Lines are longer than recommended. 79 characters on average instead of the recommended 65-75. That's my call, for density. I'm still not a hundred percent sure about it.
  • Long tables on phones. A table scrolls inside its own frame, but the header row disappears as you scroll down. Pinning it is a separate task.
  • View counts started over. The Firebase history wasn't carried over; counting starts from when Umami was installed. That matters more to me, or to potential advertisers who may or may not show up someday.

What's next

The next phase is what all this was for. A news section, interactive tools like the rack calculator, automatically generated link-preview images. After that, a public release of the theme with documentation.

If you run a blog from Obsidian on Hugo and you're thinking about a similar move, the main thing I'd recommend is this - start with your list of URLs, not with the design. A pretty site with a pile of 404s in Search Console is a bad trade. And in general, looks at the expense of function never end well - I learned that one the hard way.

item.title: Matrix Synapse - Setting Up Your Own Server for Decentralized Chat
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: Deploying Matrix Synapse in Docker with PostgreSQL behind Traefik: config generation, secure secret storage, disabled open registration, creating the first user via CLI, and connecting the Element client.
item.content:encoded:
What Matrix is and why run your own server

Matrix is an open, decentralized protocol for messaging, similar in spirit to email: every server has its own domain, and servers federate with each other, so users on different servers can talk to one another directly, with no single central company in the middle. Synapse is the reference (and by far the most widely deployed) implementation of a Matrix server, developed by Matrix.org.

For a homelab, your own Matrix server closes the same gap as any other self-hosted messenger: chats, voice and video calls, file sharing - but without depending on someone else's infrastructure and with full control over your data. Unlike fully isolated solutions such as Nextcloud Talk, though, federation optionally leaves the door open to talk to users on other Matrix servers too, including the large public matrix.org network.

The protocol itself appeared in 2014 - it was created by Matthew Hodgson and Amandine Le Pape, who came out of a corporate unified-communications project called Vector that they had worked on at Amdocs (hence the client's original name - Vector/Riot, renamed to Element only in 2018). In 2019 a separate non-profit, the Matrix.org Foundation, was set up to steward the protocol specification independently from commercial client development. The best-known case study from this history is CERN, which in 2019 began migrating roughly 18,000 employees from Skype for Business to its own Matrix/Element deployment, precisely because of the protocol's openness and the ability to keep communications fully on its own infrastructure. So this isn't some hobbyist vibe-coded project - it's a genuinely enterprise-grade technology that was originally designed with corporate needs in mind, and which we can just as well run at home.

Note

Synapse isn't the only Matrix server implementation out there (there are lighter-weight options like Dendrite and Conduit, which might actually be a better fit for a home setup), but Synapse is the most mature and best documented one, which is why this article uses it.

How Matrix differs from Telegram and WhatsApp

At first glance the difference isn't obvious - all three have chats, calls, groups, and mobile apps. Architecturally, though, these are fundamentally different things.

  • Centralization vs. federation. With Telegram and WhatsApp, every message ultimately passes through the servers of a single company (Telegram and Meta1, respectively) - no other servers exist in these networks. Matrix is a federated protocol: anyone can stand up a server, and such servers talk to each other directly, much like mail servers do for email. Your homelab server is an equal participant in the network, not a client of someone else's infrastructure.
  • Who owns the data. On Telegram and WhatsApp, messages (even when encrypted in transit) physically live on the vendor's servers. With self-hosted Matrix, your entire message history, media files, and metadata live wherever you deployed Synapse yourself - in your own Postgres database, on your own disk.
  • End-to-end encryption by default. WhatsApp turns on E2E encryption for all chats by default. Telegram only offers it in separate "secret chats," if I'm not mistaken - regular chats and groups are only encrypted in transit to the server, and the company itself is technically able to read their contents. Though honestly, I'm not 100% sure that's still accurate. In Matrix, end-to-end encryption (the Olm/Megolm protocol) can be enabled for any room, and in practice clients have long enabled it by default for private chats.
  • Open protocol and open source. The Matrix specification is open and standardized by the Matrix.org Foundation, and both the server side (Synapse, Dendrite, Conduit) and the client side (Element and others) are open source - anyone can inspect and fork them. Telegram's and WhatsApp's protocols are closed: only the company itself controls the clients and API, and third-party compatibility relies on unofficial reverse-engineering that can be cut off at any moment.
  • Resistance to blocking. Blocking Telegram or WhatsApp means blocking one specific company and its domains/IP ranges, which various countries have already tried more than once. Blocking Matrix as a whole is technically almost impossible: there are thousands of servers, each with its own domain, and blocking one server (say, the public matrix.org) doesn't touch the rest - including your own.

The practical takeaway: if convenience and an already-huge list of contacts is the deciding factor for you, neither Telegram nor WhatsApp can be replaced in one move. But if what matters is control over your data, independence from a single company's decisions, and resilience against a specific service getting blocked - that's exactly what your own Matrix server is for. And you can just as well run it for your company's employees as for your own family and friends.

What you'll need

  • a host with Docker;
  • a domain and a configured reverse proxy (Traefik, in my case) - it's used throughout this article. You can skip it and publish the port directly, but that's about the worst option available;
  • a bit of patience and time during the config- and secret-generation stage - there are many steps, but each one is fairly simple on its own.

For Synapse's database we'll use PostgreSQL rather than the built-in SQLite. This isn't a matter of taste or convenience. The developers explicitly warn that SQLite is only suitable for testing and isn't fit for real-world use because of performance limits under concurrent access. In plain terms: put more than two or three people on the server and SQLite's integrity is already at risk.

Step 1. Generate the initial config

Synapse can generate a working homeserver.yaml for you. We'll use the same image, but with the generate command. This is a one-off run of the image purely to generate the working config, not a persistent service.

Create the folder structure:

Create the temporary file with sudo nano docker-compose.yaml, just for generation:

Warning

SYNAPSE_SERVER_NAME isn't just the domain the service happens to run on - it's the server name that will forever be tied to the identifiers of all your users (@user:matrix.stilicho.ru) and to room addresses. You can't change it after the first run - or rather, you technically can, but only by creating a new server. So no, there's no migrating it. Or, to put it another way: yes, there's no migrating it. If you're unsure, pick the domain in advance and for good, including whether it'll be a dedicated subdomain (as in this article) or a bare domain without a subdomain, linked in a specific way via .well-known delegation - more on that below.

Run the generation:

The data folder will now contain a ready homeserver.yaml, along with automatically generated matrix.stilicho.ru.log.config and matrix.stilicho.ru.signing.key files - the latter is a cryptographic key the server uses to sign outgoing federation events. Guard it like the crown jewels.

Once generation is done, the temporary compose file is no longer needed - on to the real one.

Tip

Say your server needs to respond on a second-level domain (@user:stilicho.ru) rather than a subdomain - technically Synapse still has to physically run on a separate subdomain (for example, the same matrix.stilicho.ru), and the bare domain needs to be "delegated" to it via two files: https://stilicho.ru/.well-known/matrix/server and https://stilicho.ru/.well-known/matrix/client, each returning JSON with the address of the real server. That's a separate topic this article doesn't get into - for a first server, it's simpler and more reliable to just use the subdomain as-is.

Step 2. Edit the generated homeserver.yaml

Open data/homeserver.yaml and make a few edits.

Switch to PostgreSQL. As mentioned above, the generated config uses SQLite by default, so remove the sqlite block and paste in the following instead:

  • host: synapse_db - this is the name of the Postgres service from the compose file (see step 3); Docker's built-in DNS resolves it automatically within the shared network, so there's no need to hardcode any extra IP address.
  • password - must exactly match the POSTGRES_PASSWORD value from the compose stack's .env file - these are two independent places holding the same password, and letting them drift out of sync is the single most common reason Synapse fails to connect to the database after the first run.

Disable open registration. By default the key is entirely absent from the generated file, so add it explicitly:

Without this step, anyone who learns your server's address can register their own account. On a home server, we'll create users manually instead, with a dedicated command (see step 6).

Caution

The generated file already contains three secrets: registration_shared_secret, macaroon_secret_key, and form_secret. Synapse generates these randomly on the first run - unlike ready-made demo configs floating around the internet (say, in other people's docker-compose example repos), where these values can be identical for everyone who copied the file without a second glance. If you're porting a config from someone else's example, be sure to regenerate your own values, for instance with openssl rand -hex 32, and don't reuse whatever was written in the example.

The remaining keys (server_name, pid_file, listeners, media_store_path, signing_key_path, trusted_key_servers) were generated correctly and don't need touching.

Step 3. The final docker-compose.yaml

Let's go over how this differs from what Synapse generates "out of the box" in examples found online:

  • networks: synapse and proxy - synapse is an internal network purely for talking to Postgres, created automatically; proxy is Traefik's external network (external: true), which must already exist (docker network create proxy, if it hasn't been created for other services yet). The synapse_db database only sits on the synapse network - nobody outside Synapse itself needs to reach it.
  • labels - the same pattern used across the site's other articles that use Traefik as a reverse proxy: an HTTP router that redirects to HTTPS, an HTTPS router with the cloudflare TLS resolver (swap in your own resolver's name if it's different), and a load balancer pointed at the container's internal port 8008 - that's the port Synapse listens on for HTTP by default.
  • POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS - forces the database's encoding and collation to C/UTF-8 at first initialization. It's important to do this right at the start.
  • ./postgres:/var/lib/postgresql/data - a bind mount instead of a named volume, following the same approach as my other deployment examples. The path on the host is spelled out explicitly, which makes backups easier.

The .env file next to the compose file:

Warning

The POSTGRES_PASSWORD value here must be exactly the same as what you set for password inside database.args in homeserver.yaml back in step 2. Don't commit .env to git - if you manage configs via GitOps (see the article on Forgejo and Komodo), add .env to .gitignore.

Bring the stack up:

On the first run, Postgres initializes its data structures, and Synapse may restart once or twice while waiting for the database to become available - that's normal.

Step 4. Check that the server is up

Open https://matrix.stilicho.ru in a browser - Synapse serves a simple page with text like "Welcome to the Matrix," which is a sign the server is running and Traefik successfully reached it.

A more thorough check is the federation tester from the Matrix.org project itself: https://federationtester.matrix.org/ - enter matrix.stilicho.ru there, and if everything is configured correctly (including DNS and the certificate), the test will show a green federation status, even if you don't plan on talking to external servers just yet.

Step 5. Log rotation

By default, the log_config generated in step 1 is set up to rotate by size, but it's always worth checking the actual contents of data/matrix.stilicho.ru.log.config - among other things, it sets the log level (INFO by default, which is more than enough for a home server; DEBUG will quickly balloon into gigabytes of data that's useless for a home user).

Step 6. Create the first user

Since open registration is disabled (step 2), we create users manually with the built-in script inside the container:

The script asks for a login, a password, and - as a separate question - whether to grant admin rights. It only makes sense to grant admin rights to yourself; other users don't need them for ordinary use.

Note

Under the hood, the script uses the very same registration_shared_secret from homeserver.yaml - which is exactly why registration through this command still works even when the enable_registration: false config line blocks registration through every other route.

Step 7. Connect a client

The official client is Element (web, desktop for Windows/macOS/Linux, mobile apps for Android/iOS). The first time you sign in on any version of the client:

  1. Choose Sign in.
  2. Change the default server domain (matrix.org) to your own - there's usually a button like Edit next to the server address field.
  3. Enter https://matrix.stilicho.ru.
  4. Enter the login and password created in step 6.

From this point on, the server and client are linked - you can use the web version, the desktop app, and the mobile app all at once, under the same account.

What's next

What's shown here is a minimal working setup. There's plenty of room to grow from here:

  • Voice and video calls. The topic turned out to be big enough for its own article, which is coming soon - "Voice and Video Calls in Matrix - Deploying LiveKit and Element Call". Spoiler: a plain TURN server (coturn) isn't the main path to calls anymore - modern clients like Element X have moved to the MatrixRTC architecture with a LiveKit backend;
  • Bridges to other messengers (Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord) - these let you read and write to other networks straight from a Matrix client;
  • A dedicated media repository service, if the volume of forwarded files and images starts growing;
  • Backups - at minimum, the data folder (config, keys, media) and Postgres dumps; the actual backup tools are covered in separate articles on the site.

But for a first introduction to running your own Matrix server, what's shown above is, in my view, enough: a working server behind Traefik, secure secrets, disabled open registration, and a connected client.

Links

  • Official Synapse documentation
  • Synapse repository on GitHub
  • Federation Tester
  • Element client

Footnotes

  1. The organization has been designated as extremist and its activities are banned in the Russian Federation. ↩

item.title: Auto-Updating Docker Containers - Renovate + Forgejo + Komodo
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: I set up Renovate to scan docker-compose files on its own, open PRs in Forgejo with new image versions, and let Komodo redeploy the stack automatically after merge.
item.content:encoded:
If you've got more than a dozen containers in your homelab, you've probably run into the problem of how to actually keep them updated:

  • go through every docker-compose.yml by hand every couple of months and check image tags;
  • install some flavor of Watchtower and hope an automatic update of a :latest-tagged container doesn't break something important at the worst possible moment;
  • run Diun, which checks for new image versions and notifies you - but doesn't remove the need to update manually.

There's a fourth, much more interesting option: pin images to specific versions and automate the update-checking process itself. Once a week, a bot scans every compose file you've committed to your Forgejo git repository, finds new tags, and opens a Pull Request with a changelog - and you decide whether to merge it right away or read the release notes first. After the merge, deployment happens without you lifting a finger.

Note

Ideally, you'd also wire up an n8n automation to notify you in some messenger whenever an update shows up, along with a quick assessment of how important it is.

In this article I'll walk through how I put this together on my own infrastructure: Forgejo as the git server, Renovate as the bot that finds updates, Komodo as the layer that manages Docker stacks and picks up changes after merge.

This article is a direct continuation of Forgejo + Komodo - Turning Docker Compose into GitOps, where I moved all my docker-compose stacks into a single monorepo, stilicho/youtube, on Forgejo, and set up a webhook that lets Komodo pull and redeploy changed stacks after every push to main. Komodo itself as a management panel gets its own separate article, Portainer to Komodo Migration - Full Setup Walkthrough. Renovate doesn't replace or touch either of those components - it just adds one more way to land changes in main besides your own commits: it opens a PR, and once that's merged, the same webhook you already have fires. If you haven't read those two articles, some of the terminology and the repo layout here won't be obvious.

Note

Domains, usernames, and paths in the examples below are for demonstration only (stilicho.ru, user stilicho) - just swap in your own values.

Architecture

flowchart LR
    A[Renovate<br>Forgejo Action] -->|once a week<br>scans compose files| B[(Repository<br>stilicho/youtube)]
    B -->|opens a PR<br>with a new image tag| C{Review}
    C -->|merge into main| B
    B -->|webhook on push| D[Komodo]
    D -->|Pull Repo +<br>Batch Deploy Stack If Changed| E[Docker host]

Key idea: Renovate and Komodo don't know anything about each other directly. Renovate just opens PRs against the git repository. Deployment on merged code was already set up earlier - through the Forgejo → Komodo Procedure webhook (Pull Repo + Batch Deploy Stack If Changed). So there's really only one new component here: Renovate itself.

Setting up a test stack

Testing Renovate and immediately checking it against real stacks is a bad idea: if something goes wrong on the first run (say, automerge accidentally left on for a major update), you'd rather see a test nginx container break than Traefik, which routes every bit of traffic in your homelab. So before setting up the bot itself, spin up a separate, disposable stack - by the time Renovate is up and running, you'll already have a live target to test against instead of an abstract idea.

1. Add a demo stack pinned to a deliberately old image version. In the same stilicho/youtube repository, create a demo-nginx folder with a real compose file rather than an abstract placeholder - behind Traefik, with the same label pattern used everywhere else on the site:

One detail here is technical, not cosmetic: the image tag is explicitly pinned to 1.24.0 instead of being left as plain nginx (which resolves to nginx:latest). Without a specific version, Renovate can't propose anything - latest has no "next" version to bump to, so Renovate simply ignores images tagged that way. 1.24.0 is a real, but long-outdated tag (nginx dropped the separate stable/mainline branches back at 1.25 - it's all one release line now, so by the time you're reading this the current tag has almost certainly moved well past this one), so once Renovate is running, it's guaranteed to find an update - you won't have to guess whether the scan even works.

NGINX_HOST/NGINX_PORT and the volume mounted at /etc/nginx/templates are a built-in feature of the official nginx image: template files in that folder get run through envsubst and turned into a real config under /etc/nginx/conf.d, substituting in those environment variables. For a clean Renovate test this is overkill - a plain default page would do just fine - but since the stack is a real one behind Traefik anyway, it might as well look like something you'd actually deploy, not just a throwaway test.

2. Get the file into the repository. The method doesn't matter - just like with traefik/whoami in the GitOps article, you can create the file directly in the Forgejo web UI (+ New File → path demo-nginx/docker-compose.yml → paste the content → Commit Changes to main), or from a terminal:

All that matters is the result - the file needs to land on the main branch of stilicho/youtube, however it gets there.

3. Register the stack in Komodo. The push alone doesn't deploy anything yet - the deploy-on-push webhook, which we'll set up later alongside Renovate, only reacts to changes in stacks Komodo already knows about, and it doesn't know anything about demo-nginx yet. Set up a Stack resource exactly like in the GitOps article: Resources → Stacks → Create Stack, name it demo-nginx, Select Repo and point it at the same stilicho/youtube Repo resource, and set Run Directory to demo-nginx.

Warning

Don't skip the File Paths field - by default Komodo looks for a file named compose.yaml, and ours is called docker-compose.yml. Without spelling out the filename here, the deploy will fail validation with Missing files: compose.yaml, even though the file is physically there - just under a different name. See the GitOps article for the full breakdown of Run Directory vs File Paths.

Note

The same form also has Poll for Updates / Auto Update / Full Stack Auto Update toggles - leave them alone for this scenario. That's a separate, independent Komodo mechanism for images on a floating tag like :latest: once a day it checks the registry by digest and optionally redeploys. Our tag is pinned explicitly and changes through a git commit from Renovate, not through a digest change on the same tag - Komodo's own docs say it outright: "Auto-update requires a 'rolling' image tag like :latest. For pinned tags in git-sourced stacks, consider Renovate" - meaning for version pinning these are two mutually exclusive approaches, not "turn both on just in case." Flipping these toggles won't do anything here - the actual redeploy mechanism is the Pull Repo + Batch Deploy Stack If Changed webhook we'll set up in Step 7.

Save and hit Deploy once by hand - this is the first deploy, there's no webhook yet.

From this point on, demo-nginx is just another stack Komodo knows about, and it'll get picked up by the same deploy-on-push Procedure as everything else, with no extra setup later. Check that the stack actually came up - either in the Komodo UI or directly on the host:

This should return nginx:1.24.0. If the container isn't there, the problem is in the Forgejo→Komodo pipeline from the previous article, not in Renovate - there's no point going further until that part is sorted out.

The demo stack is deployed and waiting for its update - now let's move on to setting up Renovate itself.

Step 1. Bot account in Forgejo

  1. Create the account. Don't use your personal account - set up a separate renovate-bot user (Admin Panel → Users → Create User). This screen only asks for a login, email, and password. A dedicated bot account gives you two benefits: the PR history immediately shows which changes were automated, and you can scope the bot's access down to just the repository it needs.

  2. Grant access to the repository. This part happens under your own regular account (not renovate-bot) - log in as usual and go into the repository with your stacks, the one that belongs to you and that Renovate should watch. Inside it: Settings → Collaborators → Add Collaborator → enter renovate-bot (the user you created in step 1) → in the access-level dropdown that appears, pick Write.

Step 2. Access token

Log in as renovate-bot and create an Access Token (Settings → Applications → Generate New Token) with these scopes:

  • read:repository, write:repository
  • read:user
  • read:organization
  • write:issue

You'll need this token in the next step as the RENOVATE_TOKEN secret.

Warning

Without read:organization, Renovate fails with 403 Forbidden: GET /api/v1/orgs/<owner> and token does not have at least one of required scope(s): [read:organization] - it queries that endpoint to check whether the repository's owner is an organization, even with RENOVATE_AUTODISCOVER=false and the repository named explicitly in RENOVATE_REPOSITORIES.

Step 3. Forgejo Actions runner on the docker host

Renovate will run as a regular workflow rather than a standalone service - which means you need a registered runner on the host with your docker stacks. If you already set up a runner for building the site (like I did in the CI/CD article), the binary installation process is the same, just on a different host. Runner registration itself has changed since then, though - here's the current way to do it.

Download and install the binary, and create a dedicated user:

Forgejo binaries are signed with the project's GPG key - worth verifying before running anything on your host under a dedicated user that has access to the Docker socket:

You should see Good signature from "Forgejo <contact@forgejo.org>". If you get BAD signature instead, the file was corrupted or tampered with in transit - delete it, re-download, and don't proceed until it checks out.

Note

The WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature! line you'll see below that is normal and has nothing to do with the file's integrity. It just means you personally haven't signed this key into your own GPG web of trust (nobody does that for a one-off binary check) - not that anything is wrong with the signature itself. What matters is the Good signature from line and the fingerprint matching the one you requested from the keyserver (EB11 4F5E ... C592 3710).

Caution

A lot of articles and videos about Forgejo Actions still show forgejo-runner register --instance ... --token ... --name ... - an interactive registration flow with a server address and a one-time token from the web UI. This command is officially marked as deprecated right in Forgejo's own documentation - it still works, but it's no longer the recommended path. The current approach is declarative, with no interactive prompt, and happens in two steps on two different machines.

You can get the UUID + secret pair through either of two equally valid methods - pick whichever is more convenient, the rest of the article doesn't care which one you used.

Step 3.1, option A: via CLI on the Forgejo side. Log into the host where Forgejo itself runs (in my setup, that's a docker exec into its container) and run:

  • --scope - the level at which the runner will be visible: you can specify an organization, a user, or, as here, a specific owner/repo. Since Renovate only works with a single monorepo of stacks, there's no point registering the runner for the whole instance.
  • --secret - that 40-character hex string, generated ourselves via openssl rand -hex 20 (20 bytes = 40 hex characters), not something to make up by hand.
  • The command prints out a UUID in response - you'll need to copy it along with the secret for the next step.

Step 3.1, option B: through the web UI, no console at all. Runners in Forgejo have four levels at which they can be registered - pick the page that matches the --scope you'd use in option A:

  • Whole instance - https://forgejo.stilicho.ru/-/admin/actions/runners (requires instance admin rights). Not useful for this scenario - Renovate only works with one repository.
  • Organization - https://forgejo.stilicho.ru/org/<org>/settings/actions/runners, if the repo with your stacks belongs to an organization rather than a personal account.
  • Personal account - https://forgejo.stilicho.ru/user/settings/actions/runners - the runner will be visible to all of your repositories at once.
  • A specific repository - https://forgejo.stilicho.ru/stilicho/youtube/settings/actions/runners - this level is exactly equivalent to --scope stilicho/youtube from option A, and it's the one I'm using.

From any of these pages, the sequence is the same:

  1. Log in under your own regular account (not renovate-bot - registering a runner has nothing to do with the bot's repository permissions, it's a separate thing entirely).
  2. Open the page that matches your scope and click Create new runner.
  3. Enter renovate-runner as the name (the optional description field can stay blank).
  4. Click Create, and Forgejo immediately shows a page with a ready-made UUID and secret (generated automatically - no need to type anything through openssl here).
  5. Copy both values - they go into config.yaml in the next step, the exact same place the values from option A would go.
Note

The secret is only shown once and isn't stored anywhere in plain text afterward - if you close the page without copying it, you'll have to delete that runner registration and create a new one.

Step 3.2. Write the resulting values into the runner's config. This step can only be done through the console - the Forgejo web UI won't help here, regardless of whether Forgejo, Komodo, and your docker stacks all live on the same host or on different ones. It's not about the network between machines - it's that the Forgejo web UI is a browser-based application that simply has no feature for writing arbitrary files to a server's filesystem, including the runner's config.yaml. This can only be done with shell access - SSH or a local console:

Note

runner is a dedicated system user we created earlier (useradd --create-home), and its home directory /home/runner isn't readable or editable by your own regular account - only root and runner itself have access. Plain nano /home/runner/config.yaml under your own login will fail with Permission denied. From here on, use sudo for anything you need to read or edit under /home/runner - it grants the root privileges needed to get past that restriction.

The file generate-config produced isn't a short, empty template - it's the full example config, several hundred lines long, with every section and a detailed comment for each field (the same thing you'd see if you opened it yourself). You don't need to understand all of it - just three specific spots need changing, everything else can stay as generated. Open the file:

First spot - the runner: section, labels field. It's empty by default:

Replace it with a list containing one label - this is what the workflow in step 6 will use to find this runner (renovate.yml will have runs-on: docker, and the part before the colon needs to match):

The image used as the job's wrapper is node:22-trixie - Debian 13 (trixie) is currently the active stable branch.

Second spot - the server: section, connections field. In the generated file it's at the very end of the server: section and empty by default - everything above it (# example:, # codeberg:) is commented out and just for illustration, leave it alone:

Right below that line, indented two spaces further than connections:, add your own block - forgejo here is just a key for this connection (call it whatever you like, it doesn't affect behavior), followed by the three values from the previous step:

Third spot - the container: section, docker_host field. Renovate runs inside the renovate/renovate container via a docker-in-docker executor, and by default the runner doesn't mount a Docker socket into the job container at all - the generated file has:

"-" means "don't mount any docker host" - with that value, the job can't reach Docker at all. Change it to "automount" so the runner finds and mounts whatever Docker socket is available on the host:

Save (Ctrl+O, Enter) and exit (Ctrl+X).

Warning

On top of the docker_host change in the config, the runner user separately needs to be in the docker group on the host itself - we already did that with sudo usermod -aG docker runner during installation. Without both of these (the docker group and docker_host: "automount"), a Renovate job won't be able to reach Docker.

The systemd unit for the runner is already prepared in the official repository - no need to write it by hand, just download it and point it at your config file:

By default the unit points to /home/runner/runner-config.yml - the sed above swaps it for the file we generated in step 3.2 (config.yaml). From there it's the usual routine for a new unit file - reload systemd and enable the service:

Check that the runner actually started and connected to Forgejo through its logs:

Step 4. Secret in the repository

The secret goes into the same repository with your stacks (stilicho/youtube) - that's where the workflow will run, and that's where it'll need the bot's token to reach the API. Log in under your own regular account (not renovate-bot - repository secrets don't have a separate concept of "owner," they're visible to anyone with admin rights on the repo, and renovate-bot doesn't and shouldn't have those): go into stilicho/youtube → Settings → Actions → Secrets → add RENOVATE_TOKEN with the bot's token value from step 2.

Step 5. Renovate config

In the root of that same repository with your stacks (stilicho/youtube - the same one you added the secret to on the previous step), add a renovate.json:

A couple of notes:

  • No "platform": "forgejo" in this file - and that's intentional, not an oversight: platform is a global self-hosted-config option, it belongs in an environment variable (RENOVATE_PLATFORM: forgejo in the workflow, step 6), not in renovate.json, which describes settings for one specific repository. Duplicate it here and Renovate logs WARN: Found renovate config warnings - it still runs, but it's noise you don't need.
  • managerFilePatterns (the current name for this option - it used to be called fileMatch, and the old name still works but is deprecated, with Renovate offering to open an automatic Config Migration PR if it spots it) under docker-compose matters if, like me, you keep all your stacks in one monorepo: the regex needs to catch files at any depth, not just in the root. Note the slashes around each pattern (/.../) - without them the string is treated as a glob instead of a regex, and matches something else entirely.
  • ignorePaths - my .env files are committed to the repo as-is (it's a private repo), so I explicitly exclude them from scanning, just as a precaution.

For Forgejo (as a Gitea fork), people used to use the gitea platform module, but Renovate has had a dedicated forgejo module for a while now (the one we set in the RENOVATE_PLATFORM variable back in step 6) - the maintainers explicitly warn that support through the gitea module will be removed eventually, so we might as well use the correct name from the start (it works fine on both the 15.x LTS branch and 16.x - the Forgejo version doesn't matter here).

Step 6. Workflow

The workflow itself is just a regular file in the same repository with your stacks (stilicho/youtube). The path matters: it's .forgejo/workflows/, not .github/workflows/ - if you've previously migrated a workflow over from GitHub Actions, that's the first thing that changes. The file contents are identical either way - the only difference is how you get it into the repo: option A through the console, option B directly in the browser.

Option A: through the console. Clone the repository locally (or open it in an existing clone), create a .forgejo/workflows/ folder in the repo root, and drop renovate.yml in there:

File contents:

Commit and push the file under your own regular account (not renovate-bot - this is a one-time commit you make yourself, by hand):

Option B: right in the web UI, no cloning needed. Unlike step 3.2 (where the file lived on the runner's local disk), the repository itself is exactly what the Forgejo web UI is built for, so it works here without any caveats:

  1. Go into the stilicho/youtube repository under your own regular account and open the main branch.
  2. Click + (or Add File → New File, depending on the interface version) and type .forgejo/workflows/renovate.yml straight into the path field - Forgejo will create both missing folders on its own.
  3. Paste the file contents from the block above into the built-in editor (it has YAML syntax highlighting and a preview mode too).
  4. Scroll down to "Commit Changes" and commit directly to main (no separate branch or PR, same as option A).

Both options give you the exact same result - the only difference is which tool you use.

After the commit (either way), Forgejo will pick up the new workflow on its own - there's no separate step to register or "enable" it, all that matters is that the file lives at the right path on main. To confirm it was picked up, check the Actions tab of the repository - you'll see an entry for renovate.yml there even before it's ever run.

Caution

Pin the renovate/renovate image to a specific version rather than :latest. Renovate occasionally has regressions specifically around Forgejo/Gitea support (for example, schema errors with organizations that have no email set on the account) - if a version suddenly breaks, it's much easier to roll back one tag in the workflow than to figure out what changed. Check for updates every month or two and bump the version by hand.

Step 7. Deployment - already done

And here's the whole point of this setup: there's nothing to configure in Komodo specifically for Renovate, because deployment was already built earlier, in the GitOps article. Quick recap of the mechanics from there:

  1. A Renovate PR gets merged into main of the same stilicho/youtube repository that Komodo already watches.
  2. Forgejo fires the same webhook on push to main that's already wired up to the Komodo Procedure deploy-on-push.
  3. The Procedure runs Pull Repo (pulls the changed compose files) and Batch Deploy Stack If Changed (redeploys only the stacks where an image actually changed - not everything at once).

As far as Komodo is concerned, a commit from Renovate is technically no different from one of your own commits - it has no idea who actually merged the PR. That's exactly why the whole setup stays so simple: Renovate and Komodo don't know about each other directly (as I mentioned in the architecture section), and git plus the webhook you already had is what ties everything together.

Testing on the demo stack

The demo-nginx stack is already deployed (see the "Setting up a test stack" section above) and waiting for its update - now you can test the whole Renovate → Forgejo → Komodo chain end to end.

1. Force-run Renovate. Don't wait for the Saturday cron - trigger the workflow manually from the repository's Actions tab (workflow_dispatch) and watch the runner logs. Renovate will walk through every docker-compose.yml/compose.yaml in the repository (including demo-nginx) and compare image tags against the registry - but a PR might not actually show up.

Warning

"schedule": ["every weekend"] in renovate.json doesn't restrict when the bot itself runs - it restricts when it's allowed to create PRs. If you hit force-run outside the weekend, Renovate will happily find the nginx update, but instead of a PR it'll create (or update) a "Dependency Dashboard" issue in the repository - enabled by default since Renovate v26 through the config:recommended preset we're extending. Inside that issue is a list of checkboxes for updates it found but held back:

  1. Open the "Dependency Dashboard" issue in the repository.
  2. Check the box next to the nginx update line - that's the "create this PR now, ignore the schedule" command.
  3. Trigger the workflow again via workflow_dispatch - only on that second run will Renovate read the checked box and actually open the PR. Checking the box by itself doesn't create anything.

2. Merge the PR and confirm the stack was updated. The same webhook fires again - this time as a normal, fully automatic run, since Komodo already knows about demo-nginx. Komodo redeploys the stack with the new tag:

If the version in the output changed, the entire Renovate → Forgejo → Komodo chain works end to end - from spotting an outdated image to an actual redeploy, with no manual step after the merge.

Tip

If the merge commit is already sitting in the repo's history (visible on the PR page as Merge pull request ... into main), but docker inspect still shows the old tag - open the demo-nginx Stack page in Komodo and hit Refresh. This is confirmed directly in Komodo's source code: the button calls the RefreshStackCache API method, documented as "Trigger a refresh of the cached compose file contents" - Komodo keeps a cached view of the stack's state (including what it considers the "current" image for Batch Deploy Stack If Changed comparisons), and that cache updates periodically or through this exact method, not automatically the instant Pull Repo fetches a new commit. Refresh forces Komodo to re-read the files right now instead of waiting for the next cache cycle.

3. Remove the demo stack. It was only there for testing - once the check passes, delete the demo-nginx folder from the repository and commit (the same webhook fires once more), then delete the demo-nginx Stack resource itself from Komodo by hand - Delete Stack.

From there, the loop works exactly the same way on real stacks: a PR shows up → you check what changed → you merge it → Komodo redeploys everything on its own.

What's next

Some obvious improvements from here:

  • Grouping updates through packageRules - for example, one PR for every image in a stack instead of a pile of small ones.
  • Automerge for non-critical services and patch updates - carefully, and only where a breaking change is unlikely.

More on that in a future article.

item.title: GitLab, Gitea, and Forgejo. A Comparison for Grown-Ups - What Actually Fits Your Homelab
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: Comparing GitLab CE, Gitea, and Forgejo on licensing, hardware requirements, project governance, and CI/CD - and explaining why the advice to "just use GitLab, everything else is for people who don't know better" has nothing to do with actual engineering arguments.
item.content:encoded:
Under my video on setting up Forgejo and Komodo from scratch, someone left a comment along these lines: I don't know what I'm talking about, you should only use GitLab, everything else is wrong, will break, who even knows who builds this stuff, looks cobbled together, and so on. Judging by the extremely narrow worldview and the obvious lack of understanding of what homelabbing even is, the commenter was convinced their own opinion was simply correct, and that picking any git server other than GitLab was just plain dumb.

The problem with a claim like that is simple - nothing backs it up. So below is a comparison of all three products by their actual properties: licensing, hardware requirements, who runs each project and how, and what each one can really do. After that, everyone can decide for themselves who's "uneducated" here - someone who picked a tool to fit their task, or someone going off someone else's opinion in the comments.

Three products, three different audiences

  • GitLab - an enterprise-grade platform. Community Edition (CE) is free and open source, Enterprise Edition (EE) is paid, with proprietary parts. It historically bet on being "everything in one place": repos, CI/CD, security scanning, project management.
  • Gitea - a lightweight self-hosted git server written in Go, built to be a fast, low-overhead alternative to GitHub/GitLab. A fork of the older Gogs project, around since 2016.
  • Forgejo - a fork of Gitea itself, created at the end of 2022 after the domains and trademark for Gitea were handed over to a for-profit company, Gitea Ltd, without community sign-off. The community decided the fork's home would be the nonprofit Codeberg e.V., and since early 2024, Forgejo hasn't been a "soft fork" anymore - it's its own project, deliberately diverging from Gitea.

Comparison table

Criteria GitLab CE Gitea Forgejo
License MIT (CE), EE - proprietary/source-available MIT, but with a mandatory CLA on new code MIT, no CLA
Governed by GitLab Inc. (for-profit) Gitea Ltd (for-profit) Codeberg e.V. (nonprofit)
Minimum hardware 8 vCPU / 16 GB RAM (official baseline for a single node) 2 CPU / 1 GB RAM for a small team, runs fine even on a Raspberry Pi Comparable to Gitea - around 1 GB RAM to get started
CI/CD Built-in, the most mature of the three GitHub Actions-compatible syntax, added relatively recently Forgejo Actions, same syntax as Gitea's
Federation (ActivityPub) None No work, nothing announced Experimental: federated repo starring and ActivityPub HTTP signatures already work; full issue/PR federation is in progress, funded by an NLnet grant
Main use case Large teams, enterprise requirements, built-in security scanning Simple self-hosted git with minimal overhead Same as Gitea, but with an emphasis on open governance and transparency

GitLab - powerful, but expensive in resources

GitLab CE really is a free, open platform (MIT license), and that's not a marketing trick that falls apart once you look closer - only the Enterprise Edition code is closed. But all that power comes with a price: GitLab's own documentation names 8 vCPU and 16 GB of RAM as the baseline for a single-node install, and even in "memory-constrained" mode, it doesn't go below 8 GB. In practice, a fresh install with a single project will happily eat several gigabytes of RAM at idle, before any real load even shows up.

For a company running a dedicated server for GitLab, that's a fair price to pay for built-in CI/CD, security scanning, and project management in one box. For a homelab, where GitLab is competing for resources with a dozen other services on the same box, that's a real constraint - not because GitLab is "bad," but because it's built for an entirely different scale of problem. A very different one. Completely.

Gitea - light, but with some governance baggage

Gitea really is a solid example of a lightweight git server: 2 cores and 1 GB of RAM is enough for a small team, and the project officially runs even on a Raspberry Pi. The core is MIT-licensed, which is open on paper.

But it's exactly the governance side of things that sparked the conflict in 2022 that led to Forgejo existing at all (which, to be fair, is pretty much how it always goes in the Linux crowd). Gitea got itself an owner - a for-profit entity, Gitea Ltd, which took over the domain and trademark without public community sign-off, and the project started drifting toward an open-core model: some new features are built under non-free licenses, and contributors now have to sign a CLA (Contributor License Agreement) even for code that ultimately ships under MIT. That doesn't make Gitea technically "bad" - it's still actively developed and still works fine - the issue is more about how the project is governed, and not everyone in the community is on board with the overt commercialization.

Forgejo - the same code, a different governance model

Forgejo inherited Gitea's lightweight footprint (same Go stack, similar hardware needs - roughly a gigabyte of RAM to get started), but settled the governance question differently. The project's steward is the nonprofit Codeberg e.V., no CLA is required to contribute, and the whole development cycle happens on Forgejo's own infrastructure and Forgejo Actions, not on someone else's GitHub.

As of early 2024, it's a full hard fork - the codebase keeps diverging from Gitea further and further, not just syncing up with minor tweaks. Among the practical differences the project claims: end-to-end and upgrade tests (which, per the project itself, Gitea doesn't have equivalent coverage for), advance notice of security releases for everyone rather than just paying customers, and federation over the ForgeFed protocol on top of ActivityPub - still experimental (federated repo starring and HTTP signatures on ActivityPub endpoints already work, full issue/PR federation is in progress funded by an NLnet grant), while Gitea still isn't doing anything on that front.

I'll be upfront: some of this comparison comes from Forgejo's own page, so it's not an independent source. And honestly, I haven't done a full independent investigation myself. But the fact that the fork exists specifically because of a change in how Gitea is governed - that part is just history, not spin.

About that "it'll break" claim

This is where some random commenter's take parts ways with actual reality. All three products are production-grade systems with years of history, active development, and real large-scale deployments behind them. GitLab runs at thousands of companies. Gitea is the backbone of plenty of self-hosted git platforms. Forgejo, even though it's younger as its own project, is the same battle-tested Gitea code under new management - not a startup built from zero.

"It'll break" isn't a technical argument about any specific product - it's a generic line for trolling (at least that's how I read it), and it applies equally poorly to all three of them. If something does break in a real-world install, it's almost always a config mistake or a mismatch between available resources and the job at hand (see the GitLab section above), not some inherent unreliability in the software.

So what should you pick

  • GitLab if you already use it at your day job on a large team and want to practice on the same stack, or if you genuinely need the built-in enterprise features (advanced project management, security dashboards) - and have the hardware to back it up.
  • Gitea fits if you want the simplest, most time-tested option, and the governance/CLA questions don't matter much to you. On top of that, there's a huge amount of videos and write-ups about Gitea already out there.
  • Forgejo if governance transparency matters to you, you don't want to sign a CLA to contribute, and you like that the project builds itself on its own infrastructure instead of GitHub's. This is what I actually run - I covered the install and setup here, and a real working pipeline built on Forgejo and Komodo here. Spoiler: the plan is to keep walking down Forgejo's crooked "wrong" little path - documenting every step on video, obviously.

Bottom line

Picking a git server for a homelab is a question of matching resources and priorities to the actual job. GitLab is objectively more demanding on hardware. Gitea and Forgejo are technically close, and the real difference between them is who governs the project and how - not which one "breaks" and which one doesn't. If you've got solid engineering reasons for any of the three, great, let's talk about them. But the "everything else is for people who don't know better" line isn't an argument.

item.title: When Simpler Doesn't Mean Better - Going Back to Two Forgejo Repositories
item.dc:creator: Stilicho2011
item.description: Why self-hosted GitHub Actions on a single repository (article 3) turned out not to be the choice worth keeping - and how I reverted back to the proven two-repository Forgejo setup, walking through an honest comparison of both options along the way.
item.content:encoded:
The outcome of article 3 - and the first doubts

In the third article of the series I merged prohomelab-content and prohomelab-site into a single prohomelab-pages-new repository, set up a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner right on the LXC, and in the end the whole cycle - from a note in Obsidian to a published article - ended up working fully automatically. On paper, that was an improvement. Or so it seemed. One repository instead of two, no workflow_dispatch bridge between them.

In practice, over the course of one evening I ran into: a self-hosted runner that refuses to start as root; confusion between GitHub's built-in Jekyll auto-builder and my own workflow; an actual bug in Hugo itself with the published field; and - the most unpleasant part - an NTFS junction that Obsidian simply doesn't display, which for a few minutes made it look like all my articles had disappeared. Nothing was actually lost irrecoverably (git history doesn't go anywhere), but emotionally it was the most nerve-wracking part of the entire series.

Once everything was working, I honestly asked myself: was it worth it? I compared both options point by point:

Option 3 (article): self-hosted GH Actions, single repository Option 2 (articles 1-2): two repositories on Forgejo
Repositories 1 (prohomelab-pages-new) 2 (prohomelab-content, prohomelab-site)
Who builds self-hosted runner on LXC, registered in GitHub forgejo-runner on the same LXC, a different process
Runner security risk via PR on public repos (I have no pull_request trigger, but it needs to be kept in mind) Forgejo is private - no risk from public forks
Obsidian sparse-checkout, extra content/posts nesting level plain clone, flat structure, no nesting
Battle-tested yes, but only for one evening yes, this is exactly what already worked reliably before
Weak points PAT tokens on Windows, runner's systemd service, hand-written TOML workflow_dispatch between repositories, git push from CI into GitHub Pages

The conclusion didn't favor the new option: it delivers a fairly modest gain (one repository instead of two) at the cost of noticeably more places where things can go wrong. The old setup is more mundane - and that's exactly why it's more reliable.

The revert - bringing content back to Forgejo

The first problem with reverting - during the experiment I kept writing in Obsidian, and all the new content (edits to a good couple dozen articles, drafts of "Docker vs Podman vs Kubernetes," "Quadlets vs Podlets," the second article of the series, a corrected date in the Arcane post) existed only in prohomelab-pages-new on GitHub - it wasn't in prohomelab-content on Forgejo.

The fix was a plain rsync without --delete, to guarantee nothing gets erased, only added:

git status before committing is a required step, not a formality: in my case it showed not just the expected edits but a couple of surprises too - duplicated files with a " 1" suffix (looks like typical Obsidian behavior when the same note conflicts in two places) and an extra nested folder. Nothing critical, but better to see it before the commit than after.
